Since you're actually learning German, I'll mention that you WILL see "Juden" with the masculine singular. Certain masculine nouns, often those ending in -e, actually have an -en ending in the oblique cases (the non-nominative cases).

So, for example:

• Der Jude sieht mich. but Ich sehe den Juden. (accusative case)

• Der Jude klaut mir das Geld. [the jews steals my money] but Ich klaue dem Juden das Geld. [I steal the jew's money.] (dative case)

• Der Jude trinkt des Babys Blut. [the jew drinks the baby's blood] but Der Mann vergießt des Juden Blut. [The man spills the jew's blood.] (genitive case)

This is called a weak noun. They're all masculine apart from a single exception: the heart/das Herz (in dative and genitive).

• Der Hund liegt mir am Herzen. [the dog is near to my heart, lit. the dog lies on/at my heart]

It's not a huge deal, but if you learn them it will clear up the confusion you would have when encountering such special instances and if you can faithfully reproduce them in speech your German will sound very good to the native speaker.
